questions.question: What should be decided before an application stores a value in Redis?
options: Only the shortest possible key name
The value's authority, freshness, durability, and placement contract
A universal one-hour TTL
Whether every command can run on every cluster node
questions.explanation: Redis can be a disposable cache, durable state store, coordination aid, or event system. Correctness depends on making authority, staleness, loss tolerance, and placement explicit for each key family.

questions.question: A service performs 80,000 cache reads per second at a measured 95% hit rate. How many steady reads per second reach the source before retries?
questions.explanation: The miss rate is 5%, so 80,000 x 0.05 = 4,000 source reads per second. Cold-start demand can still approach the full 80,000.

questions.question: What happens with a volatile eviction policy when no keys have a TTL?
options: Redis evicts any least-recently-used key
Redis converts all keys to expiring keys
The policy behaves like noeviction for memory-growing writes
Redis automatically doubles maxmemory
questions.explanation: Volatile policies choose only keys that have an expiration. With no eligible keys, Redis cannot evict one and memory-growing writes fail as they do under noeviction.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes RDB and AOF persistence?
options: RDB is a point-in-time dataset snapshot; AOF records write operations for replay
RDB synchronously replicates every command; AOF creates hash slots
RDB guarantees zero data loss; AOF stores only read commands
They are cache eviction policies
questions.explanation: RDB periodically captures dataset state, while AOF records mutations that can be replayed. Their loss windows, recovery behavior, disk work, and backup plans differ.

questions.question: What guarantee does WAIT provide after a Redis write?
options: It turns Redis into a strongly consistent CP database
It proves a requested number of replicas acknowledged the replication bytes, reducing but not eliminating failover loss
It waits until an RDB backup reaches object storage
It guarantees Sentinel will promote a specific replica
questions.explanation: WAIT can prove that more copies received prior writes, which narrows the loss window. Redis documentation explicitly warns that it does not create strong consistency or guarantee failover retention.

questions.question: Why would keys use the same Redis Cluster hash tag, such as user:{42}:profile and user:{42}:cart?
options: To encrypt the user identifier
To force both keys into one of the same 16,384 hash slots for a multi-key operation
To replicate the keys to every primary
To bypass maxmemory
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster hashes the substring inside braces. Co-locating related keys in one slot permits supported multi-key commands, transactions, or scripts, but can also create a hot slot.

questions.question: A consumer must replay events after a disconnect and acknowledge completed work. Which Redis primitive fits?
options: Pub/Sub
A String with no TTL
A Stream with a consumer group
The SLOWLOG
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub is at-most-once and disconnected subscribers miss messages. Streams retain ordered entries and consumer groups track delivery and acknowledgments; handlers must still tolerate redelivery.
